entries.meaning: A sage respectfully recounts some of Raghupati's virtues, then, judging Bhushundi fit, begins to teach nondual Brahman: unborn, one without a second, qualityless, indwelling, partless, desireless, nameless, formless, directly knowable, undivided, incomparable, beyond mind, stainless, imperishable, changeless, limitless and a mass of bliss. The Vedas declare that this is Bhushundi and there is no difference between That and him, as between water and its wave. Though the sage explains in many ways, the formless view does not enter Bhushundi's heart. Bowing, he asks instead for embodied worship: his mind is a fish in the water of Rama-devotion, so how can the skilful sage separate it? He asks for instruction by which he may see Raghuraya with his own eyes; after filling his eyes with the Lord of Ayodhya, he will hear the formless teaching. The sage again tells Hari's matchless story, refutes the embodied view and expounds the unqualified Absolute, while Bhushundi stubbornly rejects it and argues for the embodied Lord. Their repeated answers mark the sage's body with anger: even a knower's heart can grow angry under great disrespect, just as vigorous rubbing brings fire from sandalwood.

Bhushundi reflects through rhetorical maxims: can one who seeks everyone's welfare be miserable, one who owns the philosopher's stone be poor, a malicious person be fearless or a sensualist unstained? Can a lineage survive harming a Brahmin, action remain after the Self is known, good sense arise in wicked company or an adulterer find a good end? Can a reviler of the Supreme cross becoming, a reviler of Hari ever be happy, rule endure without policy, or sin remain where Hari's deeds are told? Can pure fame arise without merit, disgrace without wrongdoing, any gain equal devotion praised by Veda, saint and Purana, or any loss equal failing to worship Rama after gaining a human body? No sin equals slander and no dharma equals compassion. Thinking such arguments, he fails to receive the sage's teaching and repeatedly presses the embodied position. Angered, the sage calls him a fool who ignores instruction, brings endless objections, distrusts truth and fears everyone like a crow. Since his heart exalts his own side, the sage curses him instantly to become the outcaste bird. Bhushundi receives the curse upon his head without fear or dejection.

Bhushundi says the sage bears no fault: Raghubansha's ornament, who prompts all hearts, clouded the sage's understanding to test Bhushundi's love, then restored it after recognizing him as his own in thought, word and deed. Seeing Bhushundi's great composure and exceptional trust in Rama's feet, the sage marvels and repents, calls him respectfully, consoles him in many ways and joyfully gives him the Rama-mantra. The compassionate sage teaches meditation on Rama's child-form, so beautiful and blissful that Bhushundi first described it to Garuda. He keeps Bhushundi there for a time and then recites the Ramcharitmanas. He had received this beautiful secret lake of Rama's deeds through Shiva's grace and disclosed it fully because he knew Bhushundi to be Rama's own devotee; it must never be told to those without Rama-devotion. After many instructions Bhushundi lovingly bows. Touching his head with a lotus hand, the sage blesses him: uninterrupted devotion to Rama will dwell forever in his heart by the sage's grace.

The blessing continues: time, action, qualities, faults and natural disposition will cause Bhushundi no suffering. Without effort he will know Rama's subtle mysteries, public and hidden histories and ancient traditions in their many forms; his love for Rama's feet will remain ever new, and through Hari's grace no heartfelt wish will be inaccessible. A grave heavenly voice confirms the sage's words and recognizes Bhushundi as the Lord's devotee in action, mind and speech. Filled with love and freed of doubt, Bhushundi obtains leave, repeatedly bows at the sage's lotus feet and comes joyfully to his present hermitage with this rare boon. He has lived there for twenty-seven kalpas, always singing Raghupati's virtues to attentive wise birds. Whenever Raghubira takes human form in Ayodhya for devotees, Bhushundi goes there, watches the childhood sports in delight, fixes the child-form in his heart and returns. Thus he has answered why he received a crow's body and has told Garuda the immense glory of Rama-devotion.

Those who knowingly abandon such devotion and labour only for knowledge are fools who leave a wish-fulfilling cow at home and wander seeking milk from a milkweed shrub. Those who reject Hari-devotion and seek happiness by other means are fools who try to cross the ocean by swimming without a boat. Garuda rejoices at Bhushundi's words: by his grace doubt, grief, delusion and error have left Garuda's heart; hearing Rama's holy virtues has brought repose. He asks why, if saints, sages, Vedas and Puranas say nothing is as rare as knowledge, Bhushundi did not honour the sage's teaching as he honoured devotion, and what difference lies between knowledge and devotion. Bhushundi replies that both remove the sufferings born of becoming, yet sages describe a distinction. Knowledge, detachment, yoga and realization are conventionally figured as masculine and powerful, while woman is figured as naturally dependent. A steadfast detached man may renounce woman, but not one ruled by desire and sense objects; even a treasury of knowledge may become helpless on seeing a moon-faced, doe-eyed woman, for woman here represents Vishnu's manifest Maya.

Bhushundi says he is not asserting a personal bias but reporting the view of Veda, Purana and saints. Maya does not become infatuated with another feminine form, he tells Garuda; this explains the metaphor. Maya and devotion are both figured as feminine, but Raghubira loves devotion, whereas Maya is merely his dancer. Because Raghuraya favours devotion, Maya is greatly afraid of it. Rama-devotion is incomparable, independent and dwells unobstructed in a heart; seeing it, Maya withdraws and cannot exercise her power. Understanding this, realized sages seek devotion, the treasury of every happiness.

Bhushundi offers an ineffable allegory for releasing the soul. The imperishable, conscious, stainless soul—an aspect of Ishvara and naturally a mass of bliss—falls under Maya and is bound like a parrot or monkey. An unreal knot joins inert matter and consciousness, yet it is hard to untie; the soul becomes worldly and unhappy, while many scriptural remedies can tighten the tangle. By divine conjunction it may finally open. If Hari's grace installs the lovely cow of sattvic faith in the heart, that cow grazes the green grass of repetition, austerity, vows, restraint and the other good practices prescribed by scripture. Spiritual feeling is its calf; withdrawal from sense objects the tethering rope, trust the vessel and the pure mind the cowherd-servant. One milks the milk of highest dharma, boils it over the fire of desirelessness, cools it with contentment and ferments it with steadfastness. Gladness churns it with the churning rod of reflection, supported by self-control and the cord of truthful speech, producing the pure, beautiful butter of detachment. Yoga's fire burns good and bad karma into the clarified butter of knowledge, consuming the impurity of possessiveness. Clear, realization-shaped intellect fills the lamp of mind with that ghee and sets it firmly upon equanimity. From the cotton of the three states and three qualities it draws the fibre of the fourth state and makes a strong wick. Thus the radiant lamp of realization is lit, and pride and the other moths burn as they approach.

The unbroken awareness 'I am That' is the lamp's intensely bright flame. In the clear joy of direct Self-experience, the root error of becoming is destroyed; the darkness of powerful ignorance and its family beginning with delusion disappears. Illumined intellect sits in the heart's chamber to untie the inert-conscious knot. If it succeeds, the soul is fulfilled, but Maya recognizes the attempt and raises many obstacles. She sends powers and attainments to tempt the intellect; they approach with artifice, force and deception and fan the flame with the edge of their garments. A supremely discerning intellect refuses to look at them, knowing their harm. If they cannot obstruct it, the deities presiding over the senses create another disturbance. They occupy the many window-like sense doors and, seeing the winds of sense objects arrive, forcibly open the body's shutters. When that gale enters the heart, it extinguishes realization's lamp; the knot remains, the light vanishes and intellect is bewildered by the winds of objects. The sense-deities do not relish knowledge, since their constant love is enjoyment; after sense-wind makes intellect foolish, who can light the lamp again?

words: to the senses and their deities

entries.meaning: The path of knowledge is the edge of a sword: one can fall from it in an instant. Whoever completes it unobstructed reaches the supreme state of isolation, which saint, Purana, Veda and Agama call exceedingly rare. Yet that same liberation comes unasked and almost by force to one who worships Rama. Just as water cannot remain without a supporting surface despite countless devices, the happiness of liberation cannot remain apart from Hari-devotion. Knowing this, wise devotees are enticed by devotion and disregard liberation. In practising devotion, the root ignorance of worldly existence disappears without separate labour, just as the stomach's fire digests food naturally when one eats for satisfaction. Hari-devotion is so accessible and joy-giving: who could be foolish enough not to love it?

Having explained the doctrine of knowledge, Bhushundi declares the majesty of devotion's beautiful wish-fulfilling jewel. In the heart it is itself supreme day-and-night radiance and needs no lamp, ghee or wick. The poverty of delusion cannot approach; the wind of greed cannot extinguish it; the darkness of powerful ignorance vanishes and every moth-like vice is defeated. Lust and the other villains stay away. Poison becomes nectar and enemies become friends, yet without this jewel no one finds happiness; grave mental diseases that torment all beings cannot afflict its bearer, who has not even a trace of sorrow in dreams. The truly clever are those who strive well for this jewel. Though manifest in the world, it comes only through Rama's grace, and unfortunate people reject the easy means of obtaining it. Veda and Purana are holy mountains; Rama's stories their beautiful mines; wise saints know the secret, good understanding is the pickaxe, and knowledge and detachment are the eyes. Whoever searches with devotion finds the jewel that contains every joy. Bhushundi believes Rama's servant is in this sense greater even than Rama. Rama is ocean, steadfast saints the rainclouds; Hari is sandalwood, saints the breeze carrying its fragrance. The lovely fruit of every practice is Hari-devotion, which no one gains without saints; therefore association with saints makes Rama-devotion accessible.
